title: Gravitational fields
summary: Kepler’s laws, Newton’s law of gravitation, gravitational field strength and orbital motion, with (HL) gravitational potential, potential energy, equipotentials, escape speed and orbital energy.

keyterms.definition: Every pair of point masses attracts with force F = GMm/r², along the line joining them.
Force per unit mass on a small test mass, g = F/m = GM/r², in N kg⁻¹.
Lines showing the direction of force on a test mass; closer lines mean a stronger field.
For orbits around the same central body, T² ∝ r³.
Planets move in ellipses with the Sun at one focus.
A line from the Sun to a planet sweeps out equal areas in equal times.
Speed of a circular orbit, v = √(GM/r).
Work done per unit mass bringing a small mass from infinity to a point: V_g = −GM/r.
Work done bringing a mass from infinity to a point: E_p = −GMm/r.
Minimum launch speed to reach infinity with no propulsion: v_esc = √(2GM/r).
Surface of constant potential; perpendicular to field lines, and no work is done moving along it.

lessons.title: Newton’s law of gravitation and field strength

questions.prompt: The distance between two masses is tripled. The gravitational force between them becomes
questions.explanation: F ∝ 1/r², so tripling r reduces F by a factor of 9.

questions.statement: Newton’s law of gravitation applies to spherical bodies as if their mass were concentrated at their centre.
questions.explanation: Outside a uniform sphere the field is the same as that of a point mass at its centre.

questions.text: Gravitational field strength has the unit N kg⁻¹, which is equivalent to ___.
questions.explanation: 1 N kg⁻¹ = 1 kg m s⁻² / kg = 1 m s⁻², so g is also the free-fall acceleration.

questions.prompt: A planet has twice Earth’s mass and twice Earth’s radius. The surface g compared with Earth is
questions.explanation: g = GM/r²: 2/2² = ½.

questions.prompt: At what height above Earth’s surface (radius R) is g one quarter of its surface value?
questions.explanation: g ∝ 1/r²; one quarter needs r = 2R, which is a height of R above the surface.

questions.prompt: Match each law to its statement.

pairs.right: Elliptical orbits with the Sun at a focus

questions.explanation: Newton’s law explains all three of Kepler’s empirical laws.

questions.statement: Gravitational field lines point away from a mass.
questions.explanation: They show the force on a test mass, which is attractive, so they point towards the mass.

questions.text: By Kepler’s second law, a planet moves ___ when it is closest to the Sun.
questions.explanation: Equal areas in equal times means a shorter radius must be swept faster.

questions.prompt: Between Earth and the Moon there is a point where the resultant gravitational field is zero. It is
questions.explanation: Earth is much more massive, so equal field strengths require being nearer the Moon.

questions.prompt: Order the steps to find g at a height h above a planet of mass M and radius R.
questions.explanation: Distances in Newton’s law are always measured from the centre of the planet.

questions.prompt: For a satellite in circular orbit, which force provides the centripetal force?
options: The gravitational force from the planet
Its weight minus the normal force
questions.explanation: GMm/r² = mv²/r, giving v = √(GM/r).

questions.statement: A satellite in a higher circular orbit moves more slowly than one in a lower orbit.
questions.explanation: v = √(GM/r), so larger r means smaller orbital speed (and a longer period).

questions.text: Using T² ∝ r³, if the orbital radius increases by a factor of 4, the period increases by a factor of ___.

questions.prompt: Astronauts in the orbiting International Space Station feel weightless because
options: there is no gravity in orbit
they and the station are in free fall together
questions.explanation: g at that height is about 90 % of surface g; everything falls with the same acceleration so there is no normal force.

questions.prompt: A geostationary satellite must orbit with a period of
questions.explanation: It must turn with Earth to stay above one point on the equator.
This derivation of Kepler’s third law shows the constant depends only on the central mass.

questions.prompt: Match each quantity to its expression.
questions.explanation: All follow from gravity supplying the centripetal force.

questions.statement: The orbital speed of a satellite depends on its own mass.
questions.explanation: The satellite mass m cancels, so all satellites at the same radius have the same speed.

questions.prompt: Earth is about 1.5 × 10¹¹ m from the Sun with T = 1 year. A planet at 6.0 × 10¹¹ m has a period of about
questions.explanation: r is 4 times larger, so T is 4^(3/2) = 8 times longer.

questions.prompt: Why do satellites in very low orbits gradually lose height?
options: Drag from the thin upper atmosphere removes energy
questions.explanation: Atmospheric drag reduces total energy, so the orbit decays; the satellite actually speeds up as it falls.

questions.prompt: Why is gravitational potential negative everywhere at a finite distance?
options: Zero is defined at infinity and gravity is attractive, so work must be done to move a mass out to infinity
It is a convention with no meaning
questions.explanation: Positive work is needed to move outwards to V = 0, so all closer points have lower (negative) potential.

questions.text: The escape speed from a planet is given by v = √(2GM/___).
questions.explanation: Setting ½mv² = GMm/r gives v_esc = √(2GM/r), independent of the escaping mass.

questions.prompt: Escape speed compared with orbital speed at the same radius is

questions.statement: Equipotential surfaces around a spherical planet are concentric spheres.
questions.explanation: V = −GM/r depends only on r, so surfaces of constant V are spheres, perpendicular to the radial field lines.

questions.text: For a satellite in circular orbit, its total energy is ___ times its kinetic energy.
questions.explanation: E_k = GMm/2r and E_p = −GMm/r, so E_total = −GMm/2r = −E_k.

questions.prompt: A satellite moves to a higher circular orbit. Which change is correct?
questions.explanation: Total energy −GMm/2r rises towards zero; E_p rises and E_k falls.

questions.prompt: Match each expression to its quantity.
questions.explanation: Field strength is the negative gradient of the potential.

questions.statement: No work is done moving a mass along an equipotential surface.
questions.explanation: W = mΔV and ΔV = 0 along an equipotential.

questions.prompt: Moving a 2.0 kg mass from a point where V = −60 MJ kg⁻¹ to one where V = −20 MJ kg⁻¹ requires work of
On a graph of potential V against distance r, the gravitational field strength at a point is given by
options: minus the gradient of the graph
questions.explanation: g = −ΔV/Δr: the steeper the potential, the stronger the field.
